US EPA, Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water (last updated 24 Feb 2026)
Meierhofer & Wegelin, Solar Water Disinfection: A Guide for the Application of SODIS, EAWAG/SANDEC Report 06/02 (2002) - copy hosted by IRC WASH, not Eawag
Eawag, Solar water disinfection (SODIS) project page

statements.text: Boil (safest - it kills every germ)
statements.quote: CDC: 'Boiling is the best way to kill germs in water.' EPA: 'Boiling is sufficient to kill pathogenic bacteria, viruses and protozoa (WHO, 2015).' Note: 'kills every germ' is stronger than either source; 'kills the germs that cause illness' would match.

statements.text: rolling boil for 1 minute
statements.quote: CDC: 'Bring clear water to a rolling boil for 1 minute'. EPA: 'Bring water to a rolling boil for at least one minute.'

statements.text: 3 minutes in the mountains, above about 1,500 m
statements.quote: EPA: 'At altitudes above 5,000 feet (1,000 meters), boil water for three minutes.' CDC: 'at elevations above 6,500 feet, boil for 3 minutes'. 5,000 ft is about 1,500 m, but EPA's own metric figure is 1,000 m and CDC's is about 2,000 m. The lesson is less cautious than EPA's printed 1,000 m; 'above about 1,000 m' would satisfy every source.

statements.text: then let it cool, covered
statements.quote: 'Let water cool naturally and store it in clean containers with covers.'

statements.text: SODIS: clear plastic bottle of 2 litres or less
statements.quote: 'transparent plastic bottles of up to 2 litres volume' (PET preferred over PVC). CDC: 'Fill clean, clear plastic bottles with clear water.'

statements.text: lay it on its side in full sun for 6 hours
statements.quote: CDC: 'Lay the bottles down on their side and in the sun for 6 hours (if sunny) or 2 days (if cloudy).' SODIS guide: 'Expose the bottle to the sun for 6 hours if the sky is cloudless or up to 50% cloudy.'

statements.text: (2 days if the sky is cloudy)
statements.quote: 'Expose the bottle to the sun for 2 consecutive days if the sky is more than 50% cloudy.'

statements.text: It does not work in rain
statements.quote: 'During days of continuous rainfall, SODIS does not perform satisfactorily.' (recommends rainwater harvesting or boiling on those days)

statements.text: or on murky water
statements.quote: 'SODIS requires relatively clear raw water with a turbidity of less than 30 NTU.' CDC: 'Solar disinfection does not work well in cloudy water'.

statements.text: plain unscented household bleach
statements.quote: 'Only use regular, unscented chlorine bleach products' ... 'Do not use scented, color safe, or bleaches with added cleaners.'

statements.text: label says 5% to 9% sodium hypochlorite
statements.quote: 'In the United States, it will typically be between 5% and 9% sodium hypochlorite.'

statements.text: less than a year old
statements.quote: 'Locate a fresh liquid chlorine bleach or liquid chlorine bleach that is stored at room temperatures for less than one year.'

statements.text: about 2 drops per litre of clear water
statements.quote: CDC, 1 quart/liter, 5-9% bleach: 'If you have a dropper: Add 2 drops of bleach'. EPA table: 1 quart/liter, 6% or 8.25%: 2 drops.

statements.text: (4 drops if cloudy)
statements.quote: CDC: 'If the water is cloudy, murky, colored, or very cold, add double the amount of bleach'. Note: both sources also double for very cold water; the lesson does not say so.

statements.text: stir, wait 30 minutes
statements.quote: EPA: 'Stir and let stand for 30 minutes.' CDC: 'Let the water stand for at least 30 minutes before you drink it.'

statements.text: It should smell faintly of chlorine; if not, add the same amount again and wait 15 minutes more
statements.quote: 'The water should have a slight chlorine odor. If it doesn't, repeat the dosage and let stand for another 15 minutes before use.'

statements.text: Weak bleach labelled 1%: 10 drops per litre
statements.quote: 1 quart/liter, 1% bleach: 'If you have a dropper: Add 10 drops of bleach'. Note: CDC's doubling for cloudy water applies to 1% bleach too (20 drops); the lesson does not say so.

statements.text: Bleach does not kill every parasite, so boil when you can
statements.quote: 'Chemical disinfectants kill viruses and bacteria, but may not kill parasites.' Disinfectants 'do not work as well as boiling for killing some germs' (Cryptosporidium, Giardia).

statements.text: If muddy, let it settle and filter it through clean cloth first, then treat
statements.quote: EPA: 'If water is cloudy, let it settle and filter it through a clean cloth, paper towel, or coffee filter.'

statements.text: These kill germs but not chemical pollution
statements.quote: CDC: 'You cannot make water containing fuel, toxic chemicals, or radioactive materials safe by boiling or disinfecting it.' EPA: 'boiling or disinfection will not destroy other contaminants, such as heavy metals, salts, and most other chemicals.'

statements.text: avoid water near mines or factories
statements.quote: No opened source names mines or factories; it is a reasonable inference from the chemical-pollution statements above.

statements.text: Keep treated water in a clean covered container and pour it out; a hand or cup dipped in makes it dirty again
statements.source: US CDC (emergency page and Safe Water Storage page)
statements.quote: 'Store the boiled water in clean, sanitized containers with tight covers.' Safe storage container: 'Has a narrow neck or opening so water can be poured out without hands or objects entering the container.'

lessons.checker_notes: The 1,500 m altitude figure sits between EPA (5,000 ft, printed as 1,000 m) and CDC (6,500 ft, about 2,000 m); the lesson is less cautious than EPA's metric figure. The lesson leaves out doubling the bleach dose for very cold water and for cloudy water when using 1% bleach. 'Kills every germ' overstates the sources slightly. The SODIS guide was read from a copy hosted by IRC WASH. Eawag's own 2016 manual and the sodis.ch pages could not be opened. The Eawag project page that did open confirms only 'exposed to full sunlight for at least 6 h'. CDC's emergency page also gives the 6-hour and 2-day SODIS times. All quotes came through the fetch tool's text extraction.

WHO and UNICEF home ORS recipe - no WHO or UNICEF page carrying it was found or opened
WHO, Manual for the Health Care of Children in Humanitarian Emergencies (2008), ch. 3 Diarrhoea and dehydration - NCBI Bookshelf copy

Diarrhoea Treatment Guidelines including new recommendations for the use of ORS and zinc supplementation (USAID MOST Project, Jan 2005; 'Both WHO and UNICEF have reviewed and endorsed these guidelines')
Rehydration Project, home-made ORS page (not a public-health body)
WHO Regional Office for the Eastern Mediterranean, Information for the general public on oral rehydration solution (WHO-EM/CSR/594/E)
opened.quote: Half a teaspoon of salt; Six teaspoons of sugar; One litre of clean and safe drinking-water or lightly salted rice water

statements.text: 6 level teaspoons of sugar and 1/2 level teaspoon of salt per 1 litre of clean water
statements.source: Rehydration Project only (not a recognised public-health body)
statements.quote: Rehydration Project: '6 level teaspoons of sugar and 1/2 level teaspoon of salt' 'dissolved in 1 litre of clean water' - the page does not attribute it to WHO or UNICEF. The WHO/UNICEF-endorsed MOST guidelines contain no home sugar-salt recipe. The WHO 2005 manual could not be opened.

statements.text: It should taste no saltier than tears
statements.quote: 'A rough guide to the amount of salt is that the solution should taste no saltier than tears.'

statements.text: Too much salt is harmful: if saltier than tears, throw it away and mix again
statements.quote: No opened source says this.

statements.text: A packet of ORS is better still - mix it exactly as the packet says
statements.quote: Packet steps: 'Add water only. Do not add ORS to milk, soup, fruit juice or soft drinks.' 'Do not add sugar.' No recognised public-health source was opened for this.

statements.text: make it fresh each day
statements.quote: 'If the child still needs ORS after 24 hours, make a fresh solution.'

statements.text: A litre is about 5 teacups
statements.quote: 'One Litre ... - 5 cupfuls (each cup about 200 ml.)'

statements.text: Add no extra sugar, and do not mix it into milk, soup or juice
statements.quote: 'Do not add ORS to milk, soup, fruit juice or soft drinks.' 'Do not add sugar.' (said of packet ORS)

statements.text: Give small sips often, even if they vomit - keep trying
statements.source: WHO 2008 humanitarian manual; WHO/UNICEF-endorsed MOST guidelines
statements.quote: 'If the child vomits, wait 10 minutes.' MOST: wait 10 minutes, then resume more slowly. Note: the sources say to wait 10 minutes after vomiting; this lesson leaves that out (the diarrhoea lesson includes it).

statements.text: as much as they will take after every loose stool
statements.quote: 'Up to 2 years: 50 to 100 ml after each loose stool.' '2 years or more: 100 to 200 ml after each loose stool.' MOST: 'Older children and adults should drink as much as they want.'

statements.text: Keep breastfeeding a baby, and keep feeding
statements.quote: 'Continue breastfeeding whenever the child wants.' 'Continue feeding'.

statements.text: Get help if they cannot keep fluids down, have blood in the stool, sunken eyes, no urine, or become very drowsy
statements.quote: MOST return signs include blood in the stool, frequent or severe vomiting, sunken eyes. WHO 2008: 'Lethargic or unconscious', 'Sunken eyes'. 'No urine' was not found in an opened source.

lessons.checker_notes: The proposed line cannot stand as written. 'WHO and UNICEF, oral rehydration (the home recipe)': no WHO or UNICEF page with the 6 + 1/2 teaspoon recipe was found within the search budget. The only page opened that gives the recipe (rehydrate.org, Rehydration Project) is not a public-health body and does not credit WHO or UNICEF. 'WHO, The Treatment of Diarrhoea (2005)': NOT OPENED, because iris.who.int refused every fetch and no other copy opened. The recipe, the 'no saltier than tears' test, 5 teacups and 'fresh each day' need a recognised source, such as the WHO 2005 manual or a WHO/UNICEF/CDC cholera or ORS leaflet, before the line can name one. Until then the line should say the recipe is not confirmed.

statements.text: Wash hands with soap after the toilet or cleaning a child's bottom
statements.quote: 'After using the toilet' ... 'After changing diapers or cleaning up a child who has used the toilet'

statements.text: and before handling food, eating
statements.quote: 'Before, during, and after preparing food' ... 'Before and after eating food'

statements.text: or feeding a child
statements.quote: Not in CDC's list. Sphere's hygiene standard, which probably lists it, could not be opened.

statements.text: this alone prevents much illness
statements.quote: Handwashing 'can keep you healthy and prevent the spread of respiratory and diarrheal infections.' (no figure given)

statements.text: toilet or latrine at least 30 m from any well or water source
statements.source: Somalia WASH Cluster (2019); WHO 1992 sets a lower minimum
statements.quote: 'at least 30 meters away from any groundwater source.' WHO 1992: 'a minimum of 15 m between a pollution source and a downstream water abstraction point' (the lesson is more cautious).

statements.text: and downhill from it
statements.quote: Neither opened source says downhill. WHO 1992 speaks of the direction of groundwater flow (downstream), which is not always downhill.

statements.text: farther in sandy, gravelly or cracked rocky ground
statements.source: WHO 1992 (cracked rock); sand and gravel only by implication
statements.quote: In fissured ground pollution 'may flow through the fissures for several hundred metres'; in fine-grained soils travel distance may be short.

statements.text: Clean water, handwashing, and safe toilets together prevent most diarrhoea and disease
statements.quote: No opened source makes this 'most' claim.

lessons.checker_notes: WHO hand-washing guidance and the Sphere Handbook 2018 were NOT OPENED: the Sphere PDF failed on every attempt, and the interactive handbook shows only headings. The 30 m figure is confirmed by the Somalia WASH Cluster guideline (a UNICEF-led humanitarian cluster) rather than Sphere itself. WHO 1992 gives 15 m as a minimum, and it says fissured rock can carry pollution several hundred metres; '30 m' is not enough there, which the lesson's 'farther' covers only vaguely.

National Center for Home Food Preservation (Univ. of Georgia), Jerky (from So Easy to Preserve, 6th ed., 2014)
National Center for Home Food Preservation, Sauerkraut
FAO, Manual on simple methods of meat preservation, ch. 2 Simple techniques for production of dried meat (year not shown on page)
FAO, Agriculture, food and nutrition for Africa, ch. 6 Food storage and processing
University of Alaska Fairbanks Cooperative Extension, Smoking Fish at Home, FNH-00325 (rev. Feb 2021)
US CDC, Botulism: Home-Canned Foods (reviewed 25 Apr 2024)

statements.text: Drying fruit: slice thin, dry on a clean raised rack in hot, dry weather, covered from flies, until leathery or brittle
statements.quote: FAO (Africa resource book) says only that sun drying is the most common household method for fruits and vegetables; no opened source gives racks, covering or the end point for fruit.

statements.text: Grains and beans are left to dry hard
statements.source: FAO, Agriculture, food and nutrition for Africa
statements.quote: 'Dry grain well before putting it in storage. The grain must be kept dry.'

statements.text: Drying meat and fish is riskier: germs that cause serious illness survive in it
statements.quote: 'pathogenic bacteria are likely to survive the dry heat of a warm oven'

statements.text: Use lean meat only
statements.quote: 'As a general rule only lean meat is suitable for drying.' NCHFP: 'Trim and discard all fat from meat because it becomes rancid quickly.'

statements.text: cut in thin strips
statements.quote: NCHFP: 'Slice meat no thicker than 1/4 inch.' FAO: strips about 1 x 1 cm, or flat pieces up to 0.5 cm thick.

statements.text: salted first
statements.quote: Dip strips in a 14-percent salt solution 'for about five minutes and then drained'; presalting also deters flies.

statements.text: hung off the ground under a cover against flies, in dry weather only, until hard
statements.source: FAO meat manual; contradicted by USDA for sun drying
statements.quote: FAO: racks with lowest traverses 'not less than 1 m from the ground', hung on sticks under a roof, sides covered 'with insect screen', dried meat should be 'hard, similar to frozen meat'. USDA disagrees: 'Sun drying is not recommended for making meat jerky due to a lack of a steady heat source.'

statements.text: and cook it before eating
statements.quote: FAO: the meat is rehydrated, usually by boiling, which is 'in most cases combined with cooking'. NCHFP allows 'heating the dried jerky strips in an oven after the drying process' to 160 F.

statements.text: Eat it within about two weeks
statements.quote: 'Properly dried jerky will keep at room temperature two weeks in a sealed container.' (USDA: 1 to 2 months; FAO: more than six months in rain-proof storage.)

statements.text: Salting: heavy salt draws out water and preserves fish and meat
statements.quote: Opened sources use salt as a step before drying (FAO), not as a stand-alone preservative. UAF says the salt and smoke levels in lightly salted fish are 'NOT sufficient to prevent bacterial spoilage'. FAO's salted-fish source was not opened.

statements.text: about 3 tablespoons [salt] to 2 kg of shredded cabbage
statements.quote: NCHFP: 'add 3 tablespoons of salt' per about 5 pounds of cabbage. CSU: '2-2.5% salt by weight - approximately 3 Tbsp. of salt per 5 pounds of shredded cabbage.' 5 lb is about 2.3 kg; 2 kg gives slightly saltier kraut, which is the safe direction.

statements.text: kept under their own brine
statements.quote: Weights 'keep cabbage submerged under the brine and away from oxygen'; cover 'with at least 1 inch of brine'.

statements.text: the sourness protects them for months
statements.source: NCHFP; CSU (only with refrigeration or cool storage)
statements.quote: NCHFP: fully fermented kraut can be 'kept tightly covered in the refrigerator for several months'. CSU: sauerkraut 'is perishable but can store long-term if maintained safely'. Neither says months without cooling, so the lesson is less cautious than the sources.

statements.text: If a ferment is slimy, mouldy through or smells rotten, throw it out
statements.quote: Neither NCHFP nor CSU lists these signs. CSU mentions only skimming surface yeast scum. The advice is cautious but has no source.

statements.text: Smoking flavours and helps dry them, but smoke alone does not make food keep
statements.quote: 'Today's lightly salted and smoked fish is not a preserved product.' 'Most smoked products have had no preservation step.'

statements.text: it must also be salted and dried hard, or cooked through and eaten within a day or two
statements.quote: UAF: 'NEVER leave smoked fish at room temperatures.' Smoked fish must be refrigerated (10-14 days) or frozen. No opened source allows keeping cooked smoked fish unrefrigerated for a day or two. 'Salted and dried hard' agrees with FAO's dried-meat method.

statements.text: Never seal moist meat, fish or vegetables airtight - in a jar, under oil, in plastic
statements.quote: CDC: 'Refrigerate homemade oils made using garlic or herbs' ... 'Throw away any unused oils made with garlic or herbs after 4 days.' UAF: 'Even vacuum-packaged smoked fish MUST be kept refrigerated or frozen.'

statements.text: A deadly poison (botulism) grows where there is no air
statements.quote: The opened CDC page does not mention low-oxygen conditions; UAF names botulism but does not state the mechanism.

statements.text: it cannot be seen, smelt or tasted
statements.quote: 'You cannot see, smell, or taste the toxin that causes botulism.'

statements.text: If in doubt, throw it out
statements.quote: 'When in doubt, throw it out!'

statements.text: Store dried and salted food somewhere cool, dark and dry
statements.quote: 'Keep the grain cool' ... 'away from direct sunlight' ... keep 'ambient humidity very low'. FAO meat manual: store dried meat in rain-proof premises.

statements.text: keep tubers in a shaded pit or root cellar
statements.source: FAO, Agriculture, food and nutrition for Africa (pits only)
statements.quote: 'yams, cocoyams and cassava may be stored in underground pits after harvesting.' Shade and cellars are not mentioned. FAO adds that fresh cassava 'deteriorate[s] rapidly' and is best left unharvested until needed.

lessons.checker_notes: Sources disagree on outdoor meat drying. FAO describes air-drying salted lean strips on raised racks under a roof with insect screen; USDA says sun drying 'is not recommended' for jerky. The lesson follows FAO, so naming USDA in the line would imply support it does not give for that method. The smoked-food line ('cooked through and eaten within a day or two') is less cautious than UAF, which says never to leave smoked fish at room temperature. 'Months' for sauerkraut is tied to refrigeration or cool storage in both extension sources. The UNH Extension page and FAO's salted-fish material were not found or opened. CSU Extension and NCHFP give the same salt ratio. CDC 'Home-Canned Foods' supports the botulism lines; it is a fourth candidate source, left out only to keep to three.

The 'same day' protein-combining idea is supported only by a university health-promotion Q&A.

opened.name: Fouad AF et al., IADT guidelines: 2. Avulsion of permanent teeth, Dental Traumatology 2020;36:331-342 - reprint hosted by the American Academy of Pediatric Dentistry
NHS, Knocked-out tooth (reviewed 6 Feb 2025)

statements.text: Clean teeth twice a day
statements.quote: 'brush your teeth at least twice a day with fluoride toothpaste - spit after brushing, do not rinse.'

statements.text: always before sleep
statements.quote: The opened NHS page does not say when.

statements.text: a brush, chewing stick, or clean cloth on a finger all work
statements.quote: No opened source mentions chewing sticks or a cloth.

statements.text: Clean along the gum line
statements.quote: Not on the opened NHS pages.

statements.text: go easy on sugar and sweet drinks
statements.quote: 'do not have too much sugary food or drink.'

statements.text: Toothache: rinse with warm salt water and keep the area clean
statements.quote: 'Dissolve half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water.' 'use a soft toothbrush'. BUT: 'Children should not try rinsing their mouth with salt water in case they swallow it.' The lesson has no child exception, so it is less cautious than the NHS.

statements.text: Face or jaw swelling, or fever with toothache, means spreading infection - get help urgently
statements.quote: See a dentist for toothache 'with a high temperature...' or 'and your cheek or jaw is swollen'. The lesson is more urgent than the NHS, which is fine.

statements.text: Swelling round the eye or in the neck, or trouble breathing, swallowing or speaking, is an emergency
statements.quote: Go to A&E if 'the area around your eye or your neck is swollen' or 'swelling in your mouth or neck is making it difficult for you to breathe, swallow or speak'.

statements.text: hold it by the white crown, never the root
statements.quote: 'Hold the tooth by the white bit that sticks out of the gum (the crown) - do not touch the root.'

statements.text: If dirty, rinse it in milk or the person's own spit
statements.quote: 'If the tooth is dirty, rinse it gently in milk, saline or in the patient's saliva.'

statements.text: (or under cold running water for a few seconds only)
statements.quote: Neither IADT 2020 nor NHS mentions rinsing in water; both give milk, saline or saliva only. IADT 2020 calls water 'a poor medium' for storage. This appears to come from the older IADT 2012 guidance, which was not opened.

statements.text: press it gently back into its socket
statements.quote: 'Attempt to place it back immediately into the jaw.' NHS: 'Try to put it back into the hole in the gum.'

statements.text: have them bite on a clean cloth to hold it
statements.quote: 'the patient should bite on gauze, a handkerchief or a napkin to hold it in place.' NHS: bite on a clean cloth 'if it goes back in easily'.

statements.text: or carry it in milk, never dry
statements.quote: Storage 'In descending order of preference, milk, HBSS, saliva' or saline; store quickly 'to avoid dehydration of the root surface'.

statements.text: get help fast; minutes matter
statements.quote: 'See a dentist or dental professional immediately.' NHS: 'Go to a dentist as soon as possible.'

statements.text: A child's milk tooth is not put back: it can harm the tooth growing underneath
statements.quote: 'You should never put a baby tooth back in.' It 'could damage the tooth growing underneath.' IADT: 'primary teeth should not be replanted'.

lessons.checker_notes: Two fixes are needed. (1) The NHS says children should not rinse with salt water in case they swallow it; add 'adults' or 'not for small children'. (2) The 'cold running water' rinse is not in the current IADT (2020) or NHS guidance; drop it or replace it with 'or saline'. 'Before sleep', chewing sticks, cloth on a finger and 'along the gum line' have no opened source. The NHS dental-abscess page was not opened; the Toothache page covers the swelling and fever warnings. IADT was read from the AAPD-hosted reprint of the Dental Traumatology article.

statements.source: St John Ambulance, Primary survey; RCUK Adult BLS 2025

statements.text: Response: speak loudly and tap the shoulders
statements.quote: Kneel next to their chest and gently shake their shoulders, asking, 'Are you OK?', 'Can you open your eyes?'.

statements.text: Tilt the head back, lift the chin; look, listen and feel for normal breathing for up to 10 seconds
statements.quote: Airway: tilt the head back and lift the chin (paraphrase). Breathing: "Watch to see if their chest moves. Do this for 10 seconds." RCUK Adult BLS 2025 gives no time limit.

statements.text: Not breathing normally, or only a gasp now and then: start chest pushes at once
statements.source: RCUK Adult BLS 2025; St John Ambulance, Primary survey
statements.quote: "Slow, laboured breathing, as well as other abnormal patterns such as agonal gasping or panting" must be recognised as signs of cardiac arrest.

statements.source: St John Ambulance, Primary survey; RCUK First Aid 2025
statements.quote: "If they are unresponsive and breathing normally but with no bleeding, put them in the recovery position". RCUK adds: "In cases of agonal breathing or trauma, do NOT move the person into the recovery position."

statements.text: Order: Bleeding is dealt with after Breathing ('Each one comes before the next')
statements.source: St John Ambulance, Primary survey; RCUK First Aid 2025
statements.quote: SJA: "Treat life-threatening bleeding by applying direct pressure to the wound before managing their airway". RCUK First Aid: "Pay immediate attention to safety, the responsiveness of the victim, and life-threatening bleeding." Heavy (spurting, pouring) bleeding must be pressed on before the airway/breathing check, not after.

statements.text: Press hard on any heavy bleeding
statements.quote: If they are bleeding severely, you will need to control and treat the bleeding by applying direct pressure to the wound.

statements.text: Give nothing to eat or drink to someone badly hurt or not fully awake
statements.quote: MedlinePlus: "Do not give the person anything by mouth, including anything to eat or drink." RCUK: "In an unresponsive person, do not give oral sugar in any form due to the risk of aspiration".

statements.text: After a fall, crash or blow to head/back, do not move them unless in danger or must be turned to keep them breathing
statements.source: RCUK First Aid 2025 (Cervical spinal motion restriction)
statements.quote: "Minimise movement of the neck." "Airway opening, if required, always has priority over in-line immobilisation".

lessons.checker_notes: Main problem: the step order puts Bleeding last, but both named sources put life-threatening bleeding before airway and breathing. Sending for help before checking response differs from the SJA order but is not unsafe. RCUK Adult BLS 2025 gives no 10-second limit; the 10 seconds come from SJA. RCUK First Aid 2025 says not to use the recovery position after trauma; the lesson's 'do not move them unless... must be turned to keep them breathing' agrees.

statements.text: Baby breaths: head level, not tilted back; cover mouth and nose
statements.quote: "Keep the head in the neutral position in infants"; "blow steadily into the child's mouth (or infant's mouth and nose) for about 1 s,"

statements.text: Baby breaths: give small puffs
statements.quote: Source says blow steadily "for about 1 s", "sufficient to make the chest visibly rise." 'Small puffs' is not in the source and may give too little air; suggest 'blow steadily for about one second, just enough to make the chest rise'.

statements.text: If others are there, change the person pushing every 2 minutes
statements.quote: it is reasonable to switch chest compressors approximately every 2 min

statements.text: If a defibrillator can be fetched, switch it on and do what it says
statements.quote: "Anyone can use an Automated External Defibrillator (AED)." "As soon as an AED is available, attach it and follow the AED instructions."

statements.text: A person whose heart has stopped may jerk for a few seconds or gasp now and then; that is not breathing
statements.quote: "A short period of seizure-like activity may occur at the onset of cardiac arrest." Agonal gasping is a sign of cardiac arrest.

lessons.checker_notes: The sources disagree on the 5 first breaths: RCUK 2025 (UK) gives 5 rescue breaths first for children, babies and drowning. AHA/AAP 2025 Part 6 (US) starts with compressions (C-A-B) and does not give 5 first breaths. AHA's 2024 drowning update lets trained rescuers start with either. So naming AHA as a source for the whole lesson is misleading for that line. Either say the child/baby/drowning sequence follows the UK guideline, or keep AHA only for the figures it supplies (1-second breaths, 4 cm infant depth, 2-minute swaps, firm surface). 'Small puffs' for babies is not in either source; RCUK says blow steadily for about 1 second until the chest rises. 'Child: one hand' is narrower than the sources, which allow one or two hands. 'Arms straight, shoulders over hands' and 'keep going until...' were not found in the opened text, but they are standard and harmless.

lessons.source_line: Resuscitation Council UK, First Aid and Paediatric Life Support Guidelines (2025); American Heart Association, Guidelines for CPR and ECC (2025); St John Ambulance, Choking

opened.name: Resuscitation Council UK, First Aid Guidelines (2025) - Choking in an adult
Resuscitation Council UK, Paediatric Life Support Guidelines (2025) - choking
American Heart Association, Part 7: Adult Basic Life Support (2025) - FBAO
American Heart Association and AAP, Part 6: Pediatric Basic Life Support (2025) - FBAO
St John Ambulance, Choking (clinically reviewed 28/04/2025)

statements.text: Can cough, speak or cry: keep coughing
statements.source: RCUK First Aid 2025; St John Ambulance, Choking
statements.quote: "Suspect choking if a person is suddenly unable to speak or cough"; encourage coughing; back blows only "If the person is unable to cough or the cough becomes ineffective".

statements.text: Adult/child over one: stand to the side and a little behind
statements.quote: Neither opened source states where to stand for back blows. Harmless detail.

statements.text: Lean them well forward; up to 5 sharp blows between shoulder blades with heel of hand
statements.source: St John Ambulance, Choking; RCUK Paediatric 2025
statements.quote: SJA: have them lean forward, support the upper body, "give them five sharp back blows between their shoulder blades." RCUK: "Lean children and adolescents forward and give blows between the shoulder blades."

statements.text: Then stand behind, fist just above the navel, grasp with other hand, pull sharply in and up, up to 5 times
statements.source: St John Ambulance, Choking; RCUK Paediatric 2025
statements.quote: SJA: fist between the belly button and the bottom of the chest, "pull sharply inwards and upwards up to five times." RCUK: fist "between the navel (umbilicus) and the end of the breastbone (xiphoid)," pull sharply inwards and upwards.

statements.text: Keep alternating 5 blows and 5 thrusts
statements.quote: RCUK: "continue alternating five back blows with five abdominal thrusts until choking is relieved". AHA: "repeated cycles of 5 back blows (slaps) followed by 5 abdominal thrusts".

statements.text: Baby: face down along forearm, head lower than chest, up to 5 back blows
statements.quote: "Turn the infant face down on your forearm with your forearm resting on your leg." "Try to hold the head below the level of the thorax." "Support the head of the infant with your hand." (Holding the jaw specifically is not stated.)

statements.text: Baby: turn face up, up to 5 chest thrusts with both thumbs, chest held in both hands
statements.quote: RCUK: "Use the two-thumb encircling technique to perform chest thrusts". AHA: "repeated cycles of 5 back blows alternating with 5 chest thrusts."

statements.text: Baby chest thrusts on the MIDDLE of the breastbone
statements.quote: Chest thrusts are done "as advised for chest compressions, but compressing the sternum more sharply"; compressions are "over the lower half of the sternum (breastbone) in all age groups." Change to 'the lower half of the breastbone'.

statements.text: Never squeeze a baby's belly
statements.quote: Abdominal thrusts are not recommended in infants.

statements.text: Do not feel blindly in the mouth: take out only what you can see
statements.source: RCUK First Aid 2025; AHA 2025 Part 7; SJA Choking
statements.quote: "Do NOT use blind finger sweeps to try and remove a foreign body from the mouth or airway." SJA: "remove any obvious obstruction from their mouth."

statements.text: Late pregnancy or very large person: thrusts on the chest, not the belly
statements.quote: "For adults in the late stages of pregnancy with severe FBAO" and "If the rescuer is unable to encircle the person's abdomen": "repeated cycles of 5 back blows (slaps) followed by 5 chest thrusts". Not in RCUK 2025.

statements.text: If they go limp and stop responding, lay them down and start chest pushes
statements.quote: "If the person becomes unresponsive, start CPR and ensure 999 has been called." RCUK Paediatric: "Start CPR immediately with five rescue breaths as soon as the child becomes unconscious."

statements.text: Anyone given belly thrusts should be seen by a health worker
statements.quote: A person given abdominal thrusts "should be evaluated by a healthcare practitioner since complications and injuries may occur."

statements.text: Any baby given chest thrusts should be seen by a health worker
statements.quote: RCUK Paediatric 2025 gives no post-choking assessment statement in the opened text. Cautious advice, not unsafe.

lessons.checker_notes: One correction is needed: the baby chest-thrust landmark should be the lower half of the breastbone, not the middle (RCUK). The AHA is the only opened source for chest thrusts in late pregnancy or a large person. RCUK 2025 first aid does not cover this. The positioning detail ('stand to the side and a little behind') and the baby 'holding the jaw' grip are not in the opened 2025 text; RCUK says only to support the infant's head. Adding St John Ambulance supports the fist position and the 'inwards and upwards' pull, which RCUK 2025 first aid does not describe.

lessons.source_line: Resuscitation Council UK, First Aid Guidelines (2025); American Heart Association and American Red Cross, Guidelines for First Aid (2024); St John Ambulance, Severe bleeding

opened.name: Resuscitation Council UK, First Aid Guidelines (2025) - Control of life-threatening bleeding
2024 American Heart Association and American Red Cross Guidelines for First Aid
AHA First Aid Guidelines index page (shows only 2020/2019/2015 updates - not the current guideline)
St John Ambulance, Severe bleeding (clinically reviewed 08/09/2026)
St John Ambulance, Life-threatening bleed (clinically reviewed 28/04/2025)

statements.text: Press firmly and directly on the wound with a clean cloth and keep pressing
statements.quote: "Apply firm, direct manual pressure to any bleeding injury site." "In the absence of any first aid dressings, any clean material can be utilised in this way".

statements.text: If blood soaks through, press harder and add another cloth on top - do not remove the first
statements.quote: "If blood comes through the dressing, remove it and reapply pressure with a new dressing or pad to control the bleeding." (RCUK 2025 and AHA/ARC 2024 do not say to stack pads; RCUK says the dressing may need to be packed into the wound.)

statements.text: Do not lift it to look
statements.quote: Not stated in opened sources; not unsafe, but it sits awkwardly with SJA's advice to remove a soaked pad and press again.

statements.text: Clean small cuts with safe water and cover them
statements.quote: "running tap water or sterile saline solutions for wound irrigation"; cover "clean superficial wounds and abrasions with an occlusive dressing to promote wound healing."

statements.text: Something stuck in the wound: do not pull it out; press on both sides and pad round it
statements.quote: Don't pull it out; "apply pressure on either side of the object to push the edges together." (Padding round it is not mentioned.)

statements.text: Limb bleeding not controlled by firm pressure: tourniquet, do not wait
statements.quote: "Apply a tourniquet as soon as possible for life-threatening extremity bleeding". AHA: "the first aid provider should apply direct pressure followed by application of a tourniquet".

statements.text: A wide band of cloth, not string or wire
statements.quote: "it is reasonable for the tourniquet to be at least 2 in width." "Narrow tourniquets cause more pain and tissue damage." SJA: improvise with a triangular bandage, belt or tie. AHA: "A commercial tourniquet is probably superior to an improvised tourniquet."

statements.text: 5 to 7 cm above the wound and never on a joint
statements.source: RCUK First Aid 2025; SJA Life-threatening bleed
statements.quote: "Place the tourniquet around the traumatised limb 5-7cm above the injury, but not over a joint." SJA: "It should never be placed on a joint."

statements.text: Knot a stick into it and twist until bleeding stops completely, then tie the stick
statements.quote: "Tighten the rod by twisting it until the bleeding stops, and secure it in place using the rod clip." AHA: "a tourniquet should be applied and tightened until the bleeding stops."

statements.text: If it still bleeds, put a second band above the first
statements.quote: In some cases, you may need to apply a second tourniquet, above the first tourniquet, to control the bleeding.

statements.text: It hurts; that is expected
statements.quote: Tell the casualty "it will hurt when you tighten it."

statements.text: Write down the time, leave it on; only a health worker takes it off
statements.quote: "Write the time the tourniquet was applied." "Do not release the tourniquet. It should only be released by a healthcare professional."

statements.text: Armpit or groin: push clean cloth firmly into the wound and press hard
statements.quote: Apply a dressing then firm direct pressure, "which may require at some sites the dressing to be packed into the wound." (Armpit/groin not named.)

lessons.checker_notes: CONTRADICTED: St John Ambulance (reviewed Sept 2026) now says that if blood comes through, you take the pad off and press again with a new one. You do not stack pads. Suggested wording: 'If blood soaks through, you are not pressing on the right spot or hard enough: take the cloth off, find where the blood is coming from, and press again harder with a fresh cloth, or push the cloth into the wound.' AHA/ARC 2024 says a manufactured tourniquet is probably better than an improvised one; add 'use a ready-made tourniquet if you have one'. The AHA 'First Aid Guidelines' index page still shows only the 2020 focused update. The current guideline is the 2024 AHA and American Red Cross Guidelines for First Aid, so the line should say 2024. The 5-7 cm figure comes from RCUK; AHA says only 'proximal to the wound'.

opened.name: St John Ambulance, Shock (clinically reviewed 28/04/2025)
NHS first aid page - redirects to St John Ambulance; no NHS shock page found
MedlinePlus (US National Library of Medicine), Shock (reviewed 14 Oct 2025)
2024 American Heart Association and American Red Cross Guidelines for First Aid (shock position)
St John Ambulance, Broken bones and fractures (leg-raise exclusion)
WHO, Diarrhoeal disease fact sheet (7 March 2024)

statements.text: Caused by heavy bleeding, bad burns, a broken thigh or hip, or severe diarrhoea
statements.quote: "severe internal or external bleeding"; "loss of body fluids from dehydration, diarrhoea, vomiting, or burns." (Broken thigh/hip not named; covered by internal bleeding.)

statements.text: Signs: pale, cold, sweaty skin; fast weak pulse; fast shallow breathing
statements.quote: "pale skin, which may be cold and clammy"; fast pulse, weak pulse; fast, shallow breathing. MedlinePlus: "Rapid but weak pulse".

statements.text: Signs: thirst
statements.quote: Neither opened shock page lists thirst.

statements.text: Signs: feeling faint or sick, then confusion and drowsiness
statements.quote: MedlinePlus: "Confusion"; "Dizziness, lightheadedness, or faintness". SJA: nausea and possible vomiting; becoming unresponsive.

statements.text: Stop any bleeding first
statements.quote: Treat any visible or identified cause, such as severe bleeding.

statements.text: Lay them flat; raise the legs a little only if no pain and head, back, hips and legs are not injured
statements.quote: MedlinePlus: "elevate their legs about 12 inches (30 centimeters)"; "If raising the legs will cause pain or potential harm, leave the person lying flat." AHA: "raising the feet about 6 to 12 in (≈30°-45°) from supine position may be reasonable" (only with no evidence of trauma). SJA: do not raise legs if broken or pelvis/hip injured.

statements.text: Keep them warm: something under them as well as over them
statements.quote: Keep them warm with a coat or blanket, and lay them on a rug or blanket if available.

statements.text: Loosen tight clothing; stay with them and speak calmly
statements.quote: Loosen any tight clothing around the neck, chest, and waist. Reassure and keep them calm.

statements.text: Nothing to eat or drink
statements.quote: Do not give the person anything by mouth, including anything to eat or drink.

statements.text: Wet the lips if they are thirsty
statements.quote: Not in any opened source.

statements.text: Shock from diarrhoea: give ORS in sips if awake
statements.quote: WHO: "Diarrhoea should be treated with oral rehydration solution (ORS)" but: "Rehydration with intravenous fluids in case of severe dehydration or shock." WHO does not say ORS treats shock; the lesson is less cautious - shock from diarrhoea needs a drip urgently.

statements.text: Get help urgently; recovery position if unresponsive but breathing; chest pushes if not breathing
statements.quote: Call 999 or 112; "If they become unresponsive, prepare to treat them as an unresponsive casualty." MedlinePlus: "If necessary, begin rescue breathing and CPR."

lessons.checker_notes: 'UK NHS' cannot stand as a source: nhs.uk/conditions/first-aid now redirects to St John Ambulance, and no NHS shock page was found. MedlinePlus is used instead. The ORS line is the main concern. WHO says shock or severe dehydration from diarrhoea needs intravenous fluids. Suggested wording: 'Shock from diarrhoea needs a drip from a health worker urgently; while you wait, if they are awake and can swallow, give ORS in small sips.' Even that 'while you wait' step is not in the opened WHO fact sheet. SJA raises the legs on a chair, above heart level, which is higher than 'a little'. AHA/ARC 2024 allows leg raising only with no trauma, so after a serious injury the lesson's condition is less cautious than AHA but matches SJA and MedlinePlus. 'Thirst' and 'wet the lips' were not found.

lessons.source_line: British Burn Association, First Aid Clinical Practice Guidelines (2018); UK NHS, Burns and scalds; WHO, Burns fact sheet (2026)

opened.name: British Burn Association, First Aid Clinical Practice Guidelines (Pre-Hospital SIG, April 2018) - copy hosted by Salisbury NHS Foundation Trust
NHS, Burns and scalds (last reviewed 31 March 2026)
WHO, Burns fact sheet (21 October 2026)
2024 AHA and American Red Cross Guidelines for First Aid (burns - for disagreement only)

statements.text: Clothes on fire: stop, drop and roll, or smother the flames
statements.quote: BBA: Stop, Drop and Roll - "ROLL over and back and forth until the flames are out." WHO: "stop exposure to the source of heat and extinguish flames safely." (Smothering not named.)

statements.text: Cool with clean, cool running water for 20 minutes
statements.quote: "cool running tap water for 20 minutes and within 3 hours of injury." WHO: "approximately 20 minutes is commonly advised for smaller burns where this can be done safely."

statements.text: It still helps up to three hours after the burn
statements.quote: Do this as soon as possible, within 3 hours of it happening.

statements.text: No running water: lay on wet cloths and keep changing them
statements.quote: "Apply a cool water compress using any clean wetted lint free cloth," changed frequently over 20 minutes.

statements.text: Keep the rest of the person warm
statements.quote: "Keep the rest of the person warm and avoid delaying urgent treatment". BBA: "Cool the burn but warm the patient."

statements.text: Take off rings, watches, tight clothing near the burn before it swells (unless stuck)
statements.quote: Remove rings, watches and other tight items early; remove clothing that is not stuck to the wound.

statements.text: Cover loosely with a clean non-fluffy cloth or clean plastic
statements.quote: "Cover the cooled burn with loose longitudinal strips of cling film" or a clean lint-free cloth; "Do not wrap cling film circumferentially around limbs".

statements.text: Do not use ice, butter, oil or toothpaste
statements.quote: "Do not apply ice, oils, butter, toothpaste, traditional pastes or other household substances to a burn." (AHA/ARC 2024 differs: "it may be reasonable to cool superficial burns (with the skin intact) with ice wrapped in cloth" when running water is unavailable.)

statements.text: Do not burst blisters
statements.quote: do not burst any blisters.

statements.text: Chemical burn: brush off dry powder, then flood with water for at least 20 minutes
statements.quote: "Brush off dry powders"; irrigate with "room-temperature running water for at least 20 minutes." BBA caution: do not irrigate dry lime, phenols, muriatic acid, concentrated sulphuric acid or elemental metals with water. WHO: irrigate "unless specific chemical safety guidance advises otherwise."

statements.text: Get help for large or deep burns, face, hands, feet, genitals; electricity or chemical; breathed in smoke
statements.quote: "seek urgent medical care for deep, large, electrical or chemical burns," "burns of the face, hands, feet or genitals, or possible inhalation injury."

statements.text: Get help for burns on joints
statements.quote: None of the opened sources names joints. Cautious, not unsafe.

statements.text: Get help for burns in a child
statements.quote: The NHS page only says to call 111 for children under 5. AHA/ARC 2024 refers children at a lower size threshold (5% body surface vs 10%).

lessons.checker_notes: All three named sources were opened and support the lesson. The BBA document is from 2018 and was opened from a copy hosted by an NHS trust (Salisbury), not on britishburnassociation.org. The sources disagree on two points. (1) Ice: the AHA/ARC 2024 guideline allows ice wrapped in cloth for small surface burns when there is no running water; BBA, WHO and NHS say no ice. The lesson follows BBA/WHO. (2) Cooling time: AHA says 5-20 minutes; the others say 20. Two places where the lesson is less cautious than its sources. First, BBA and WHO warn that long cooling can chill infants, older people and people with large burns; the lesson says to keep the rest of the person warm but does not mention watching small children and large burns. Second, for chemicals, BBA says some (dry lime, elemental metals such as sodium, concentrated sulphuric acid, phenol) should not be washed with water; WHO says to wash 'unless specific chemical safety guidance advises otherwise'. Suggest adding 'unless the label says not to use water'. 'Joints' is not in the opened referral lists. The NHS page also lists burns on the bottom.

opened.name: St John Ambulance, Broken bones and fractures (clinically reviewed 28/04/2025)
St John Ambulance, Sprains and strains (clinically reviewed 28/04/2025)
2024 American Heart Association and American Red Cross Guidelines for First Aid
British Red Cross, First aid for a broken bone (no date shown)

statements.text: Signs: severe pain, swelling, limb bent or wrong, cannot bear weight
statements.quote: "deformity, swelling, and bruising around the fracture" and "pain or difficulty moving the area."

statements.text: Do not straighten it or push bone back in
statements.quote: AHA: "Splinting an injured extremity in the position found is accepted first aid practice." Reducing angulated fractures carries "risks, including injury to nerves." BRC: "Never attempt to put dislocations back in place". SJA: pressure around the wound "but not over the protruding bone".

statements.text: Splint it as it lies: pad something stiff and tie it on above and below the injury so the joint each side cannot move
statements.quote: AHA: "Splinting of a fractured extremity can be useful to reduce pain". SJA: support the joints above and below; "Place padding around the injury for extra support"; secure with sling or broad-fold bandages. (Improvised stick/cardboard splints not named.)

statements.text: Check fingers/toes stay warm and pink; loosen ties if numb, pale or blue
statements.quote: AHA: "If a fractured extremity is blue, purple, or pale, the emergency response system should be activated immediately." SJA asks about pins and needles or numbness. 'Loosen the ties' is not stated explicitly.

statements.text: Open break: cover with a clean cloth - urgent
statements.quote: Cover with a sterile dressing or clean non-fluffy cloth; open fractures need "immediate transfer to A&E by calling 999 or 112."

statements.text: Sprains: rest, cool early with a wet cloth, wrap snugly, raise
statements.quote: SJA: "R - rest the injured part"; ice pack or cold compress for no more than 20 minutes; "Support the injury in an elevated position". AHA: "applying a compression wrap after an acute ankle sprain or strain" "without compromising circulation"; cold "limited to 20 to 30 minutes per application".

lessons.checker_notes: The 'rest of the lesson' now has a named source: the 2024 AHA/ARC Guidelines for First Aid (splint as found, do not realign, cover open fractures, compression wrap for sprains, pale or blue limb means get help). The British Red Cross page says to use padding 'to align it, if you can, but do not force it', which is softer than the lesson's 'do not straighten'. The lesson follows the more cautious AHA position. Suggest adding a time limit to the cooling: 'about 20 minutes at a time' (SJA no more than 20; AHA 20-30).

lessons.source_line: American Heart Association and American Red Cross, Guidelines for First Aid (2024); UK NHS, Heat exhaustion and heatstroke, and Hypothermia

opened.name: 2024 American Heart Association and American Red Cross Guidelines for First Aid
NHS, Heat exhaustion and heatstroke (last reviewed 28 May 2026)
NHS, Hypothermia (last reviewed 09 June 2023; next review was due 09 June 2026)
Resuscitation Council UK, First Aid Guidelines (2025) - heat stroke, hypothermia

statements.text: Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea
statements.quote: "tiredness", "dizziness", "headache", "feeling sick (nausea)", "excessive sweating and skin becoming pale and clammy".

statements.text: Shade, sips of water or ORS, wet cloths and fanning, rest
statements.quote: "Move them to a cool place." Give water, "an isotonic sports drink or oral rehydration powder"; "spray or sponge them with cool water and fan them."

statements.text: No better after 30 minutes: treat it as heatstroke
statements.quote: Call 999 if "still being unwell after 30 minutes of resting in a cool place, being cooled and drinking fluids".

statements.text: Heatstroke: hot skin (sweating may stop), confusion, staggering, collapse
statements.quote: "hot skin that's not sweating and might look red", "confusion and lack of coordination", "a seizure or fit", "loss of consciousness".

statements.text: Cool water up to the neck, about 15 minutes or until they come round
statements.quote: "whole-body (neck-down) cool- to cold-water immersion for 15 minutes or until neurological symptoms resolve (whichever occurs first)." RCUK: "continue cooling for 15 min or until neurological symptoms resolve, whichever is first."

statements.text: No such water: shade, soak skin and clothes, fan hard, wet cloths to neck, armpits, groin
statements.quote: AHA: "evaporative, fanning, or a combination of techniques when water immersion is not available"; "application of ice packs to the axilla and groin." NHS: cold packs "under the armpits or on the neck".

statements.text: Sips only if fully awake
statements.quote: provide cool liquids if the person is able to swallow.

statements.text: Hypothermia: violent shivering at first; when shivering stops and they turn confused, clumsy and sleepy it is life-threatening
statements.quote: NHS lists "shivering", "slurred speech", "tiredness or confusion". AHA lists decreased responsiveness as a sign of life-threatening hypothermia. Neither says shivering stopping marks severity.

statements.text: Handle them gently
statements.quote: "gently remove wet clothing and replace it with dry garments". General gentle handling not stated.

statements.text: Get them dry and out of the wind, insulate all round and underneath, cover the head
statements.source: RCUK First Aid 2025; NHS Hypothermia; AHA/ARC 2024
statements.quote: RCUK: insulate with dry blankets, shield from wind, replace wet clothing, insulation between them and cold ground. NHS: wrap them "making sure their head is covered".

statements.text: Another person's warmth
statements.quote: "It is not beneficial to use body-to-body rewarming for active rewarming over other active rewarming techniques." It is an option, but less effective than other heat sources.

statements.text: Warm sweet drinks only if fully awake
statements.quote: give them a warm non-alcoholic drink and some sugary food like chocolate if they're fully awake

statements.text: No rubbing, no alcohol, no hot bath or hot bottle on the skin
statements.quote: "do not use a hot bath, hot water bottle or heat lamp to warm them up"; "do not rub their arms, legs, feet or hands"; "do not give them alcohol to drink". AHA: "Heat sources, rubbing, and massage should not be applied to the extremities".

lessons.checker_notes: The proposed line is accurate. The AHA/ARC guideline is the 2024 edition, confirmed on cpr.heart.org. The NHS hypothermia page is past its review date: it was last reviewed June 2023 and the next review was due June 2026. 'When shivering stops it is life-threatening' was not found in any opened source; AHA ties life-threatening hypothermia to decreased responsiveness. Suggest 'when they turn confused, clumsy and sleepy (shivering may stop)'. AHA says body-to-body warming is less effective than other active rewarming. That is acceptable where nothing else exists, but don't present it as first choice. Neither the RCUK 2025 nor the AHA 2024 cooling recommendation says to hold the head up; that is common sense.

lessons.source_line: Resuscitation Council UK, First Aid Guidelines (2025); MedlinePlus (US National Library of Medicine), Non-fatal drowning (2025); WHO, Drowning fact sheet (2026)

opened.name: Resuscitation Council UK, First Aid Guidelines (2025) - Drowning
Resuscitation Council UK, Paediatric Life Support Guidelines (2025)
MedlinePlus (US National Library of Medicine), Non-fatal drowning (reviewed 14 Oct 2025)
WHO, Drowning fact sheet (1 May 2026)
St John Ambulance, Drowning (clinically reviewed 28/04/2025)
AHA newsroom: 2024 AHA and AAP Focused Update on Special Circumstances: Resuscitation Following Drowning
AHA Instructor FAQs, 2024 Drowning Focused Update

statements.text: Do not go in after them if you can help from the bank
statements.quote: If you are not trained in water rescue, do not enter the water, as you might risk drowning.

statements.text: Reach with a pole, branch or rope, or throw something that floats
statements.source: MedlinePlus Non-fatal drowning; RCUK First Aid 2025
statements.quote: "Extend a long pole or tree branch to the person or use a throw rope attached to a buoyant object". RCUK: "stay on land and reach out to the person through flotation devices, a lifebuoy, a rescue tube or other rescue equipment."

statements.text: Pull them in while you lie down or hold on to something
statements.quote: Not in any opened source. Sensible, low risk.

statements.text: Use a boat if there is one
statements.source: RCUK First Aid 2025 (mentions rescue boat only as a place to give breaths)
statements.quote: RCUK: give five rescue breaths "on land or a rescue boat"; no advice to use a boat for the rescue.

statements.text: Not breathing: 5 breaths, then 30 pushes and 2 breaths
statements.quote: "If so, immediately give five rescue breaths, then begin standard CPR." SJA: "five initial rescue breaths"; "After 30 chest compressions, give two rescue breaths." (AHA 2024 lets trained rescuers start with breaths or compressions.)

statements.text: Do not waste time trying to drain water from the lungs
statements.quote: No opened source addresses draining water. MedlinePlus: "Do not perform the Heimlich maneuver unless repeated attempts to position the airway and rescue breathing have failed". SJA: be ready to roll them onto their side if they bring up stomach contents.

statements.text: Breathing: recovery position; take off wet clothes and wrap them up
statements.quote: "put them in the recovery position"; "If possible, replace the wet clothes with dry clothes." MedlinePlus: "Remove any cold, wet clothes from the person and cover with something warm, if possible."

statements.text: Anyone rescued, or who coughs or breathes hard afterwards, needs a health worker even if they seem well: lungs can fail hours later
statements.quote: "All people who have experienced a non-fatal drowning should be checked by a health care provider." "Even though the person may quickly seem OK at the scene, lung complications are common." SJA: "Medical advice should be sought, even if they appear well in the immediate aftermath."

statements.text: Most drownings are small children near home - in wells, ponds, tanks and buckets
statements.quote: WHO says "The highest drowning rates per population are among children aged 0-4 years" - a rate, not 'most drownings'. WHO names open wells and ponds as exposures; MedlinePlus names buckets and basins. 'Most' is an overstatement.

statements.text: Cover wells and tanks, fence ponds, never leave a small child alone near water
statements.quote: WHO: "Covering wells, using doorway barriers and playpens, fencing swimming pools". MedlinePlus: "Never leave children alone for any period of time or let them leave your line of sight around any pool or body of water."

lessons.checker_notes: 'Reach or throw, do not go in' now has a source: RCUK First Aid 2025 (do not enter the water if untrained; reach with flotation or rescue equipment) and MedlinePlus (pole, branch, throw rope). 'Most drownings are small children' overstates WHO, which says children aged 0-4 have the highest drowning rate. Suggested wording: 'Small children drown more often than anyone else, mostly near home...' In each case the lesson is more cautious than the source, not less. Grunting appears only on the 2014 recording form, not in the classification, and not anywhere in the 2019 booklet.

Suggested fix: state the site ('38 C in the bottom, about 37.5 C in the mouth or armpit') or use WHO IMCI's 37.5 C. The adult breathing range 12-20 is on the MedlinePlus 'Rapid shallow breathing' page, while the 'Vital signs' page says 12-18. The 35.5 C newborn figure could not be read in the 2014 IMCI copy, so cite WHO newborn recommendations 2017 (or the 2019 young-infant booklet) instead of 'IMCI 2014'. The AVPU-style alertness scale, the hand-on-chest check and counting breaths without telling them have no source among those opened.

statements.quote: Hesperian asks for 'sterile string' and gives baking as the method for string; its boiling list does not include ties. PCPNC uses 'the ties and razor blade from the disposable delivery kit'. Strips of cloth are not mentioned.

statements.text: let her walk, kneel, squat or lie on her side as she likes - not flat on her back
statements.quote: Encourage the woman to walk around freely ... DO NOT let her lie flat (horizontally) on her back.

statements.text: She should drink, eat lightly, and pass urine often
statements.quote: Encourage the woman to eat and drink as she wishes throughout labour. Encourage the woman to empty her bladder frequently. Remind her every 2 hours.

statements.text: She pushes only when she cannot help pushing
statements.quote: Allow her to push as she wishes with contractions. DO NOT urge her to push. (Hesperian: not until 'she is overwhelmed by the urge')

statements.text: Never push on her belly
statements.quote: Never push on the mother's belly to hurry the birth.

statements.text: Never pull on the baby
statements.quote: Guide the head - do not pull it. ... Do not pull on the baby.

statements.text: Put nothing into the vagina
statements.quote: Closest: some midwives do not touch the vagina at all, which the book calls 'a good practice'.

statements.text: give no herbs or medicines to hurry the birth
statements.quote: Only 'Do not give medicines to get labor started again' (twin-birth section). Herbs not mentioned in the chapters opened.

statements.text: support the baby's head as it comes, and let the baby turn by itself; the shoulders and body follow
statements.quote: Keep one hand gently on the head as it advances with contractions. (PCPNC then has the attendant 'Apply gentle downward pressure to deliver top shoulder'.)

statements.text: If a loose cord lies round the neck, slip it over the head; if it will not slip, do not pull on it - let the baby be born through the loop and unwind it at once
statements.quote: PCPNC: 'If cord present and loose, deliver the baby through the loop of cord or slip the cord over the baby's head; if cord is tight, clamp and cut cord, then unwind.' Hesperian: if it cannot be loosened, keep the head close to the mother's thigh and let the body turn out, then unwind.

statements.text: Lift the baby straight onto the mother's belly
statements.quote: put the baby on her mother's belly, skin to skin

lessons.checker_notes: Mostly supported. Not found: boiling the cord ties, and strips of cloth as ties (Hesperian sterilises string by baking). 'Put nothing into the vagina' and 'no herbs or medicines to hurry the birth' are not stated as such in the chapters opened. For a tight cord, PCPNC says to clamp and cut before birth; the lesson follows Hesperian's 'born through the loop' approach, which suits a helper with no clamps. The Hesperian files are the 2026 edition: the index footer reads 'A Book for Midwives 2026'.

statements.text: dry the baby all over with a clean cloth, take the wet cloth away, lay the baby naked on the mother's bare chest with a dry cloth over both
statements.quote: Thoroughly dry the baby immediately. DO NOT leave the baby wet ... Leave baby on the mother's chest in skin-to-skin contact. Cover the baby, cover the head with a hat.

statements.text: rub the back gently but firmly two or three times
statements.source: HBB provider guide 2016; WHO newborn recommendations 2017
statements.quote: Rub the back 2 or 3 times gently but firmly. (WHO 2017: 'stimulated by rubbing the back 2-3 times')

statements.text: wipe the mouth and nose only if mucus is blocking them
statements.quote: Suctioning should be done only if the mouth or nose is full of secretions.

statements.text: Still not breathing - act within the first minute
statements.quote: By one minute after birth - The Golden Minute - a baby should be breathing well or you should be providing ventilation.

statements.text: send someone else for help
statements.quote: CALL FOR HELP - one person should care for the mother.

statements.text: lay the baby on its back with the face straight up (the head not tilted far back)
statements.quote: Hesperian: head facing straight up, small rolled cloth under the shoulders, do not tilt the head back far. HBB: 'Reposition the head with the neck slightly extended.'

statements.text: cover the baby's mouth and nose with your mouth, and give a small puff of air from your cheeks - not a full breath
statements.source: Hesperian p. 242 ONLY (not WHO, not HBB)
statements.quote: Cover the baby's mouth and nose with your mouth ... use only as much air as you can hold in your cheeks; 'Do not blow hard into the baby's lungs'. HBB and WHO describe bag-and-mask only; mouth-to-mouth is not mentioned in either.

statements.text: about every two seconds
statements.quote: Hesperian: start with 3 to 5 slow breaths, 'Then give small, quick puffs about 3 seconds apart.' HBB (bag and mask): 'Ventilate at 40 breaths/minute (30-50 breaths/minute acceptable)' - one every 1.2-2 s. The lesson's 2 s fits neither exactly: it is at the slow edge of HBB's range and faster than Hesperian.

statements.text: just enough to make the chest rise. If the chest does not rise, move the head a little and try again
statements.quote: Check that ventilation breaths produce movement of the chest ... Reposition the head with the neck slightly extended.

statements.text: Keep going until the baby breathes
statements.quote: 'If the baby starts to cry or breathe at least 30 breaths a minute, stop rescue breathing.' Hesperian also says to stop if no breathing after 20 minutes - the lesson gives no stopping point.

statements.text: Never slap or shake a baby or hold it upside down
statements.quote: Never hit or hurt a baby or hold her upside down to make her cry.

statements.text: Wait a few minutes, until the cord has stopped beating
statements.source: Hesperian p. 214; WHO PCPNC C18 and D; HBB 2016
statements.quote: Hesperian: when no longer pulsing, usually about 3 minutes after birth. PCPNC C18: cut when it 'stops pulsating'; D: '1-3 minutes after birth'. HBB: 'Wait at least 1 minute-and up to 3 minutes'.

statements.text: Tie it tightly in two places, about two and five finger-widths from the baby's belly
statements.quote: PCPNC: 'put ties tightly around the cord at 2 cm and 5 cm from baby's abdomen.' Hesperian: first tie 'about 2 finger widths from the baby's belly', the second 'a little farther up the cord'. The lesson seems to have turned centimetres into finger-widths: five finger-widths is about 8-10 cm.

statements.text: cut between the ties with the clean blade
statements.quote: cut between ties with sterile instrument

statements.text: Put nothing on the stump - no ash, dung, oil or powder
statements.quote: 'Put nothing on the stump.' (WHO newborn recommendations 2017 also recommend daily chlorhexidine 4% on the stump for home births where neonatal mortality is high.)

statements.text: if it oozes blood, tie it again more tightly
statements.quote: Neither gives a re-tie instruction. PCPNC: 'If umbilicus is red or draining pus or blood, examine the baby and manage accordingly.'

statements.text: put the baby to the breast within the first hour
statements.source: WHO PCPNC K2; HBB 2016; PCPNC C18
statements.quote: Babies should start breastfeeding within 1 hour of birth.

statements.text: suckling helps the womb tighten and the bleeding stop
statements.quote: Breastfeeding makes the womb contract and stop bleeding.

statements.text: The afterbirth usually comes by itself within the hour
statements.quote: Stage 3 'usually lasts less than 1 hour.' PCPNC C18: 'wait for the placenta to deliver on its own.'

statements.text: Do not pull on the cord, and do not press on the womb to bring it
statements.quote: Hesperian: 'Pulling on the cord is dangerous!' PCPNC: 'DO NOT squeeze or push the uterus to deliver the placenta.' (PCPNC's skilled-attendant procedure does use controlled cord traction after a uterotonic.)

statements.text: Putting the baby to the breast, passing urine, and sitting up or squatting to push with a pain all help
statements.quote: Breastfeeding causes contractions; she should urinate; she can sit up or squat and push during contractions.

statements.text: If it has not come an hour after the baby, get help at once
statements.quote: Placenta not expelled 1 hour after birth of the baby.

statements.text: the womb should be hard, like a ball ... If it is soft, or she bleeds, rub it firmly until it hardens
statements.quote: Massage uterus to expel clots if any, until it is hard. ('Uterus not hard and not round' is a referral sign.)

statements.text: Check the womb and the bleeding every 15 minutes in the first hours
statements.quote: MONITOR MOTHER EVERY 15 MINUTES (first hour after placenta); during stage 3 'Repeat check every 5 minutes'. Hesperian: check every 1 or 2 minutes for a while, then every few hours.

statements.text: do not leave her alone on the first day
statements.quote: To NOT leave the mother alone for the first 24 hours.

statements.text: Emergency: blood pouring, or a pad or cloth soaked in less than 5 minutes; a fit; fever
statements.source: WHO PCPNC C18 and D postpartum box
statements.quote: Heavy bleeding after delivery (pad/cloth soaked in less than 5 minutes). (Postpartum box: 'more than 2 or 3 pads soaked in 20-30 minutes' - a lower threshold.)

statements.text: For bleeding rub the womb, put the baby to the breast, help her pass urine, keep her lying down and warm, and get help at once
statements.quote: Rub the womb; 'Breastfeeding makes the womb contract and stop bleeding'; urinate; for shock lie with feet higher than head, keep her warm; get medical help.

lessons.checker_notes: Two figures are wrong and one technique rests on a single source. (1) The cord ties: the sources say 2 cm and 5 cm (PCPNC), or about 2 finger-widths then a little farther (Hesperian). The lesson's 'two and five finger-widths' matches neither, and five finger-widths is roughly double the WHO distance. (2) The breath interval: Hesperian, the only source that teaches mouth-to-mouth, says puffs about 3 seconds apart. HBB (bag and mask) gives 40 a minute, 30-50 acceptable. The lesson's 2 s should be aligned with one named source. (3) Mouth-to-mouth for a newborn is in Hesperian only. HBB 2nd edition and WHO describe bag-and-mask only, so citing HBB must not imply it teaches mouth-to-mouth. HBB does support: rub the back 2-3 times, the Golden Minute, chest rise, repositioning the head, cord timing and the first-hour breastfeed. (4) 'Re-tie if it oozes' has no source among those opened. (5) Hesperian says to stop rescue breathing after 20 minutes without breathing; the lesson says 'keep going'. (6) WHO 2017 recommends chlorhexidine on the cord for home births in high-mortality settings; the lesson's 'put nothing on the stump' follows PCPNC K10 instead. HBB copy: AAP Provider Guide 2nd ed. statements.text: Warm: skin to skin with the mother, a cap on the head, dry cloths
statements.quote: Cover the head with a cap for the first few days, especially if baby is small. (2017: skin-to-skin during the first hour; clothing '1-2 layers more than adults and a hat')

statements.text: no bath on the first day
statements.quote: Bathing should be delayed to after 24 hours of birth. (PCPNC 2015 says only 'at least 6 hours' - the newer WHO text is stricter and matches the lesson.)

statements.text: A baby born small or early is kept skin to skin day and night
statements.quote: If the baby is small, encourage the mother to keep the baby in skin-to-skin contact for as long as possible, day and night. (2017: continuous Kangaroo mother care for newborns 2000 g or less)

statements.text: upright between the breasts
statements.quote: Neither opened text describes the kangaroo position.

statements.text: Breast milk only for the first six months - no water, tea, honey or porridge
statements.quote: All babies should be exclusively breastfed from birth until 6 months of age. PCPNC: 'DO NOT give any other feeds or water.' (honey not named)

statements.text: Feed whenever the baby wants, day and night, at least 8 times in 24 hours
statements.source: WHO PCPNC K; WHO IMCI 2014 p. 39
statements.quote: A baby needs to feed day and night, 8 or more times in 24 hours from birth.

statements.text: wash your hands before touching the baby
statements.quote: Always wash hands before and after taking care of the baby.

statements.text: Keep the cord stump dry and outside the nappy
statements.quote: Put nothing on the stump. Fold nappy (diaper) below stump. (2017: 'Clean, dry cord care'; chlorhexidine 4% daily for home births in high-mortality settings)

statements.text: it falls off in a week or two
statements.quote: Hesperian: the stump falls off 'usually within the first week'. PCPNC gives no timing.

statements.text: Sleep: on the back, under the net, near the mother
statements.quote: Let the baby sleep on her/his back or on the side. ... Use the bednet day and night for a sleeping baby. ... let the baby sleep with the mother or within easy reach

statements.text: Danger signs: feeding poorly or not at all; a fit
statements.quote: (1) stopped feeding well, (2) history of convulsions

statements.text: breathing 60 times a minute or more
statements.source: WHO IMCI young infant 2019; WHO 2017 ('fast breathing')
statements.quote: Fast breathing (60 breaths per minute or more)

statements.text: fewer than 30
statements.quote: Hesperian: breathing faster than 60 or slower than 30 breaths a minute, and grunting, mean the baby 'needs help'. PCPNC K11: 'breathing less than 30 per minute'.

statements.text: gasping
statements.quote: If the baby is not breathing or is gasping for breath, start resuscitation within 1 minute of birth.

statements.text: grunting
statements.source: Hesperian p. 241 (not in WHO 2017 or the 2019 IMCI young-infant booklet)
statements.quote: Signs of breathing trouble include ... grunting.

statements.text: or the chest pulling in
statements.quote: (4) severe chest in-drawing

statements.text: hot or cold to the touch
statements.quote: K14: 'fever or feels cold'. 2017: '(6) temperature >37.5 oC, (7) temperature <35.5 oC'

statements.text: floppy, moving only when stirred, or not moving
statements.quote: (5) no spontaneous movement / 'Movement only when stimulated or no movement at all'

statements.text: yellow skin on the first day, or yellow palms and soles at any time
statements.quote: Severe jaundice: 'Any jaundice in an infant aged less than 24 hours' or 'Yellow palms or soles at any age'

statements.text: bleeding or pus from the cord, or a red, swollen or smelly cord

statements.quote: Return or go to hospital immediately if the baby has: ... very small, just born

lessons.checker_notes: Well supported. PCPNC section J (the newborn examination chart) could not be found or opened, so the danger signs were checked against WHO 2017, PCPNC K14, the 2019 IMCI young-infant booklet and Hesperian. Grunting and 'fewer than 30' come from Hesperian; the WHO texts opened do not list grunting, which is why Hesperian is added. PCPNC K14 also lists 'diarrhoea' and 'skin pustules', and 'feeds <5 times in 24 hours' as reasons to go; the lesson omits them. PCPNC allows sleeping 'on the back or on the side'; the lesson's 'on the back' is narrower. The 'upright between the breasts' kangaroo position has no source among those opened. WHO's page says the 2017 recommendations are 'being updated'.
